title: Comments of Old Dominion Electric Cooperative re PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s Reliability Backstop Procurement filing under ER26-3380.

documents.name: ER26-3380 ODEC Comments.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                          )    Docket No. ER26-3380-000


              COMMENTS OF OLD DOMINION ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE

    I.   INTRODUCTION

         On July 31, 2026, as supplemented on August 14, 2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

(“PJM”) submitted revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the

Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) for a proposed

Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”). The RBP, as described by PJM, is a one-time

mechanism to address the capacity shortfall caused by large loads. The proposed RBP would

procure capacity needed to meet the reliability requirement shortfall for the 2028/2029 Delivery

Year, to the extent new loads coming online in the 2027/2028 or 2028/2029 Delivery Years do not

voluntarily procure sufficient new capacity to address the shortfall or otherwise qualify for the

limited RBP opt-out.1 PJM requests Commission acceptance and an effective date for RBP of no

later than September 29, 2026, so that PJM can commence RBP procurement on September 30,

2026.2

         ODEC respects PJM’s critical role in ensuring resource adequacy and facilitating reliable

interconnection of large loads. In that regard, ODEC does not take issue with PJM’s assessment

of the problem – there is an impending reliability problem of insufficient capacity that must be

addressed immediately, for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.3 However, as discussed in these


1
  PJM Transmittal Letter at 26.
2
  Id. at 27.
3
  See id. at 7 (“the addition of new supply has not kept pace with rapid large load demand growth, thus
giving rise to the significant tightening of the capacity market in recent years and the subsequent resource
adequacy shortfalls.”)

                                                     1
 comments, PJM’s proposed solution raises concerns regarding whether costs and risks will be

sufficiently aligned with the large loads that drive the need for the procurement. Rather than accept

PJM’s RBP as filed, the Commission should instead take PJM up on its offer for the Commission

to adopt revisions to specific elements of the RBP and adopt an alternative that received significant

stakeholder support. Specifically, the Commission should direct PJM to adopt the “subscription

model” proposed by Joint EDCs and the Data Center Coalition and approved by the PJM

stakeholders by a super-majority vote.4

       Further, the Commission should revise the proposed RBP to adopt a revision to provide

unrestricted opt-out for municipally owned utilities and electric cooperatives. At the very least,

PJM should be required to confirm that electric cooperatives such as ODEC are eligible for the

opt-out mechanism and revise the opt-out provisions as necessary to reflect such clarification.

       Finally, ODEC has identified an inconsistency between PJM’s statement in the RBP

transmittal letter and its proposed Tariff provisions with respect to allocation of RBP Charges in

the event of default by LSEs. PJM should confirm that the Tariff is what it intends for RBP Default

Allocation.

       Pursuant to the Combined Notice of Filings #1 issued August 3, 2026, ODEC submits these

comments on PJM’s RBP proposal. In support of its request for the Commission to remedy PJM’s

RBP, ODEC states as follows:




4
 The Joint EDCs and Data Center Coalition Reliability Backstop Procurement Package proposal is
available in materials posted by PJM for the June 30, 2026, PJM Members Committee meeting,
https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-groups/committees/mc (last visited August 18, 2026). For
convenience, a copy of the proposal is attached to this pleading.

                                                 2
 II.     COMMENTS

            A. The subscription model better aligns procurement obligations with cost-causation

                principles.

            PJM’s RBP will require LSEs to meet significant collateral requirements, cover the cost of

  capacity allocated to them per the allocation of RBP Charges, and bear responsibility for defaults.5

  Each of these components of PJM’s proposal will create significant financial and other obligations

  for LSEs, including the costs to administer or implement the new obligations, as well as potential

  impacts on LSEs’ ability to shoulder these costs while continuing in their other obligations. PJM

  acknowledges the region is in the predicament due primarily to the influx of large loads without

  adequate or timely investment in new generation to serve those large loads.6

            PJM’s proposal places substantial responsibility for these risks on LSEs who neither caused

  the underlying problems of large loads with insufficient capacity, nor caused these costs to be

  incurred. LSEs will bear the cost of RBP Collateral – which must be in the form of cash or a letter

  of credit deemed acceptable to PJM or PJMSettlement – that is in addition to and separate from

  collateral they already must post for the RPM auctions and bilateral transactions. Moreover, the

  amount of such collateral is unknown at this time and will not be known until after the cost

  responsibility for RBP capacity has been determined for the Delivery Year. We can expect that the

  RBP Collateral requirement for individual LSEs who will be allocated cost responsibility for RBP

  Charges will be significant. As PJM explains, the risk of non-performance for RBP resources is

  greater than the risk for resources in the RPM Auctions and, therefore, PJM has created RBP

  Collateral requirements that reflect the inherently riskier nature of RBP resources. ODEC is

  concerned that this risk will not be borne by those who cause the risk (RBP Sellers, large loads).


  5
      See PJM Transmittal Letter at 50.
  6   See PJM Transmittal Letter at 1.

                                                     3
 It will instead be shifted to LSEs. While PJM contends its imposition of the risk of default on LSEs

is consistent with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, that simply is not the case. The Ratepayer

Protection Pledge calls for large loads to cover the costs of new capacity and for costs not to

become stranded or socialized. The Ratepayer Protection Pledge does not contemplate LSEs

serving as the primary backstop for costs and risks that originate with large-load growth.

       PJM contends that it has no choice but to shift all the cost and risk to LSEs, because PJM’s

jurisdiction stops at the Electric Distributor/LSE and we must depend on the states to take it from

there. ODEC agrees that states have an important role in ensuring large loads pay their fair share

and other ratepayers are not forced to subsidize the costs associated with large loads. However,

using LSEs as the default payer, with no assurance of the level of costs or that those costs will be

allocated to large loads, does not adhere to principles of cost causation. Retail customers from

every rate class may end up paying these costs if the states do not adopt measures to ensure the

LSEs have the regulatory mechanisms to allocate these costs to those who cause them.

       PJM’s RBP relies on rules that do not exist, to define the large loads to whom these costs

will be allocated and the mechanisms for doing so. It is unreasonable to expect that the states, even

with their best intentions and resources, will be able to resolve these determinations in time for the

RBP that PJM intends to commence on September 30, so that LSEs have any of the assurance they

will not shoulder the stranded costs of default and/or RBP Charges, as well as RBP Collateral.

       PJM’s Board had another option to consider, which would have provided a mechanism to

address the shortfall in the short term without unreasonably shifting all cost and risk to LSEs. As

PJM briefly mentioned in its filing, the Joint EDC and Data Center Coalition (“Coalition”)

proposed a subscription-based model for RBP. In summary, the subscription model would have

LSEs secure bilateral contracts or other arrangements to meet the large load capacity obligations,



                                                  4
 then opt to participate in a central procurement by indicating to PJM the MW quantity that PJM

should procure on their behalf through the RBP. Those LSEs would be responsible for satisfying

the credit or collateral requirements associated with any capacity committed on their behalf

through the RBP and would not be permitted to participate in RBP if they fail to do so. Thus, the

LSE would remain responsible for protecting other LSEs and PJM market participants from

assuming obligations associated with a default. However, unlike PJM’s RBP proposal, the

Coalition RBP proposal gives LSEs the opportunity to determine how best to meet the capacity

needs of their customers, including through bilateral arrangements and contracts outside of RBP

to protect LSEs and their customers. The Coalition RBP proposal also avoids the use of a large

load forecast to procure long-term capacity commitments that is a component of PJM’s RBP

proposal. PJM acknowledges the need to improve load forecasting and has efforts underway to do

so.7 However, there is a significant risk that PJM will over-procure capacity because the RBP

Targets will be based on load forecasts that were not developed with this urgent and long-term

commitment in mind and may be outdated or contain duplicative requests. Additionally, PJM’s

approach does not provide any mechanisms to lock-in the capacity commitments made on behalf

of the large load for the possible 15 year term of the RBP. Thus, even if the large load does

materialize as forecasted, there are no assurances it will stay online for the full 15 years. The

Coalition RBP proposal’s subscription-based approach would allow LSEs who represent or serve

large load end-users, to make capacity commitments based on contracts and communications with

large loads.

          There was significant stakeholder support for the Coalition subscription-based proposal.

As PJM reported, the Coalition RBP proposal was the only one of the 13 different RBP proposals



7
    PJM Transmittal Letter at 25.

                                                 5
 that received greater than two-thirds sector-weighted member support. The PJM Board opted not

to adopt the core difference between the Coalition Proposal and the PJM RBP; the subscription

model. PJM’s RBP will impose costs and risks on LSEs that the LSEs did not cause. Therefore,

the Commission should direct PJM to adopt the subscription aspect of the Coalition RBP Proposal

if the Commission deems it is permitted to do so under FPA section 205.8

        B. The Commission should direct PJM to revise its Opt-Out or at the very least

            clarify eligibility for the Opt-Out.

        PJM proposes a RBP Opt-Out that would provide for a reduction in the Initial RBP Target

for calculating the Final RBP Target, where an Electric Distributors’ zone or area has rates that

are not regulated by the states and the Electric Distributor is unable to address cost allocation

associated with capacity procured in the RBP.9 In order to request the Opt-Out, an Electric

Distributor must not only identify the quantity of load that will be opted-out in the Initial RBP

Target, but also provide “supporting documentation demonstrating an inability to address cost

allocations associated with capacity procured in the backstop” as well as written support for the

opt-out from the state governor, RERRA and interconnection customer(s).10 In the event the

Commission does not adopt the subscription model for RBP discussed above, then the Commission

should direct PJM to revise its Opt-Out.

        PJM explains in its filing that the Opt-Out is in response to concerns raised by cooperatives

that cooperatives who are Electric Distributors in a retail choice state are not state regulated and


8
  PJM has consented to “the Commission’s exercise of authority to modify and/or sever any element of
the proposed Tariff and RAA language ot he extent necessary and permitted under section 205 of the FPA
and NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC . . .” PJM Transmittal Letter at 3. ODEC expects that PJM
would not find the subscription model consistent with PJM’s RBP, even if FERC deems it is permitted to
direct such a revision while accepting PJM’s filing. In that instance, the Commission should reject PJM’s
filing as unjust and unreasonable.
9
  PJM Proposed Tariff Section 18.1(d).
10
   Id.

                                                   6
 not otherwise serving as the LSE for generation to load, would not have a state regulatory authority

to address the allocation of RBP costs to other large loads or zones within the state.11 As discussed

above, ODEC has significant concerns that as an electric cooperative that will be subject to RBP

Charges, ODEC and its member distribution cooperatives will be left to bear the costs for RBP

Charges, defaults, and RBP Collateral without assurance that it will be able to allocate those costs

to large loads who cause the costs to be incurred.

          ODEC appreciates PJM’s effort to address concerns raised by electric cooperatives and

municipal utilities regarding mandatory participation in RBP. As PJM explains, the opt-out

provision was developed in response to concerns that certain entities could be required to bear the

costs of capacity procured for large loads that ultimately fail to materialize. PJM further explains

that cooperatives and municipal utilities may face unique challenges because they are not always

subject to traditional state rate regulation.

          ODEC believes, however, that the underlying purpose of the opt-out is broader than

addressing a narrow regulatory gap. The concern raised by cooperatives was fundamentally one of

risk allocation: ensuring that smaller, community-focused utilities are not required to assume

procurement obligations and associated financial risks that may be outside of their control. Rate

regulation status may be one factor relevant to that concern, but it is not the concern itself. In

ODEC’s view, PJM’s discussion appears to rely on the premise that electric cooperatives and

municipal utilities generally are not subject to rate regulation. While that may be true in some

jurisdictions, it is not universally the case. For example, Virginia’s electric cooperatives operate

under a regulatory framework that includes oversight of rates and services by the Virginia State

Corporation Commission. The existence of such oversight demonstrates that the distinction is not



11
     PJM Transmittal Letter at 45.

                                                 7
 as simple as whether an entity is or is not rate regulated. More importantly, the procurement and

cost-allocation risks that motivated the opt-out can exist regardless of the specific form of

regulatory oversight applicable to a utility.

          ODEC therefore believes the opt-out was intended to provide a reasonable safeguard for

smaller utilities, including electric cooperatives and municipal utilities, that could face

disproportionate exposure to Reliability Backstop Procurement obligations. Interpreting the

provision solely through the lens of traditional state rate regulation risks narrowing the opt-out

beyond the concern it was designed to address. The Commission should instead evaluate the opt-

out consistent with its broader purpose of protecting smaller utilities from undue procurement risk

while preserving flexibility for those entities best positioned to manage that risk.

          Electric cooperatives and municipals have every reason to ensure sufficient capacity and

that costs are allocated to the large loads who cause those costs to be incurred. PJM’s willingness

to provide the opt-out demonstrates that PJM agrees or at least does not oppose the ability of

electric cooperatives to secure sufficient capacity outside of the RBP. Therefore, if the

Commission accepts PJM’s RBP, it should condition such acceptance on a compliance filing by

PJM to remove the restrictions on the opt-out and instead provide an unrestricted opt-out for

electric cooperatives and municipal utilities. This change is consistent with the goal of PJM’s Opt-

Out provision and, therefore, can be required per PJM’s advanced consent to the Commission’s

authority to modify the proposed Tariff and RAA language.12 Specifically, the Commission should

direct PJM to submit a compliance filing to revise the RBP Opt-Out, as follows:

          (d) Opt-Out

       When calculating the Final RBP Target, the Initial RBP Target shall also be decremented
where the Electric Distributor’s zone/area has rates that are not regulated by the states and is unable
to address cost allocation associated with capacity procured in the backstop includes load that is
12
     PJM Transmittal Letter at 3.

                                                  8
 served by an electric cooperative or a joint municipal agency, upon request by the Electric
Distributor to opt-out a portion or all of its associated portion of the Initial RBP Target. Such
request by the Electric Distributor shall specify the associated MW quantity of load in the
zone/area that will be opted-out of the Initial RBP Target and be accompanied by supporting
documentation demonstrating an inability to address cost allocation associated with capacity
procured in the backstop, along with written support for such opt-out from the relevant state
governor, RERRA, and interconnection customer(s). The Initial RBP Target shall be further
decremented, if requested by an Electric Distributor, by up to the associated MW quantity of load
that participates in a peak shaving adjustment program where such Electric Distributor’s zone/area
addresses their capacity needs through peak shaving adjustment programs that are codified in state
law and that also meet the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-2.

       Additionally, PJM should clarify that for purposes of the Opt-Out, generation and

transmission electric cooperatives qualify for the opt-out, as opposed to only their distribution

cooperative members. ODEC is the LSE for its member cooperatives. ODEC is also presumably

the entity that will receive the RBP Charge and RBP Collateral obligations. Therefore, ODEC

should be permitted to request the RBP Opt-Out. ODEC is not subject to rate regulation by state

commissions but is instead subject to rate regulation at FERC. However, its member distribution

cooperatives in Virginia are subject to state regulation by the Virginia State Corporation

Commission. The PJM RAA defines Electric Distributor as follows:

       “Electric Distributor” shall mean a Member that 1) owns or leases with rights
       equivalent to ownership of electric distribution facilities that are used to provide
       electric distribution service to electric load within the PJM Region; or 2) is a
       generation and transmission cooperative or a joint municipal agency that has a
       member that owns electric distribution facilities used to provide electric distribution
       service to electric load within the PJM Region.

       Based on the definition of Electric Distributor, ODEC is an Electric Distributor because

ODEC is a generation and transmission cooperative that has members that own electric distribution

facilities used to provide electric distribution service to electric load in the PJM Region. PJM

should clarify that ODEC and other similarly situated generation and transmission cooperatives

qualify for the Opt-Out, even if their distribution cooperative members are state regulated.




                                                 9
              C. PJM should resolve an inconsistency in its filing.

             PJM states in its transmittal letter that if an LSE defaults and fails to pay an RBP Charge,

   “PJM will allocate the defaulted amount to all remaining LSEs that have been assigned

   responsibility for RBP Charges in the Electric Distributor zone/area based on each LSE’s pro-rata

   share of the total RBP Charges, as allocated based on either the Reliability Backstop Obligation

   or PJM’s back-up cost allocation methodology.”13 However, the proposed Tariff states that the

   defaulted amount “will be allocated to all remaining Load Serving Entities responsible for paying

   RBP Charges based on their pro rata share of the total RBP Charges for all such Load Serving

   Entities. . .”14 The difference between these two can be significant, because allocating default

   amounts to only the zone as opposed to all LSEs in the PJM Region could result in LSEs in the

   default zone bearing a larger portion of the default amounts. ODEC presumes that PJM’s Tariff

   would control, but PJM should confirm its intent to allocate default amounts to all LSEs in the

   region with responsibility for RBP Charges.

III.     CONCLUSION

             WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, ODEC requests that the Commission consider

   these comments in its determination of the PJM RBP proposal and if the Commission accepts the

   filing, require PJM to submit a compliance filing to (1) adopt the “subscription model” proposed

   by Joint EDCs and the Data Center Coalition; (2) in the event the Commission does not adopt the

   subscription model, then revise PJM’s proposed RBP to provide an unrestricted opt-out for

   municipally-owned utilities and electric cooperatives and confirm that electric cooperatives such

   as ODEC are eligible for the opt-out mechanism and revise the opt-out provisions as necessary to




   13
        PJM Transmittal Letter at 90 (emphasis added).
   14
        Proposed Tariff Section 18.9.

                                                         10
 reflect such clarification; and (4) confirm that the Tariff reflects PJM’s intention for the RBP

Default Allocation.

                                                   Respectfully submitted,

                                                                                     ATTACHMENT




            Joint EDCs & Data Center Coalition (“Coalition”)
                Reliability Backstop Procurement Package
                                Executive Summary
Joint EDCs = Buckeye Power, Dominion Energy, Duke Energy Ohio, Duke Energy Kentucky,
Duquesne Light Company, East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Exelon, Old Dominion
Electric Cooperative, PPL Electric Utilities Corp., Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative



The Coalition supports and include PJM’s bilateral matching phase in our package. The
process provides opportunities for large loads and suppliers to directly contract to add
needed capacity to the RTO system while allowing for negotiated terms and conditions to
be decided among the parties. A strong bilateral contracting phase will improve the
likelihood of success of the central procurement proposed by the Coalition.

The Coalition supports PJM implementing a centralized procurement to address the
capacity needs of Large Loads, a Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP), centered on two
core principles:

       1. Establishing a subscription-based procurement target which recognizes the
       benefit of Large Loads continuing to secure bilateral contracts that manage risk
       within contract terms outside of PJM’s markets, and

       2. Ensuring that RBP costs and credit/collateral obligations are assigned to the
       appropriate cost-causing parties at the time RBP commitments are made.

A Load Serving Entity (LSE) is the entity legally or contractually obligated to supply a Large
Load’s capacity and energy needs. LSEs, therefore, should be responsible for both
determining the procurement target for the Large Loads they serve and bearing associated
financial and credit obligations associated with those loads.

The Coalition’s proposal is grounded in PJM’s existing legal and operational framework.
Under PJM’s governing documents, LSEs that rely on PJM markets must be parties to the
Reliability Assurance Agreement (RAA) and are responsible for financial obligations arising
from RPM capacity auctions. LSEs work with the loads they serve to determine how best to
satisfy capacity obligations, including making resource build, demand response, and
bilateral contracting decisions. A central RBP must accommodate the ability of the LSE to
determine how best to meet the capacity needs of its customers, including respecting
                                              1
                                                                                      ATTACHMENT




RERRA directives for how those needs should be satisfied. Any RBP should respect LSE
decisions that may transfer cost and financial risk outside of the PJM market by allowing
the LSEs to opt-into the procurement. There simply is insufficient time to ensure all
bilateral contracting that that can be completed before PJM intends to conduct the RBP.

The Coalition proposes that the LSEs who wish to participate in the central procurement (or
Large Loads themselves if they so desire) would indicate the MW quantity PJM should
procure on their behalf through the RBP. This may be referred to as a subscription model.
The decision to subscribe is based on the legal arrangement between the LSE and the
relevant Large Load. In subscribing, the LSE commits to satisfying the credit/collateral
requirements at the time the RBP commits supply resources and through the duration of
the RBP resource commitment period. An LSE that cannot satisfy the credit requirements
described below is not permitted to subscribe MW to be procured through the RBP. This
protects other LSEs and PJM market participants more broadly from assuming obligations
should a default of an RBP obligation occur of the RBP obligation were to occur. This
approach also should accommodate Large Load switching to new LSEs, with their
subscribed RBP commitment following them to their new LSE.

The registry-based subscription model proposed by the Coalition simultaneously
addresses concerns related to over procurement, cost allocation and cost shifting.



LL LSE Registry

To establish the procurement target, the Coalition proposes the creation of a Large Load
Registry, maintained by PJM, through which either the Large Load or its designated LSE
would report:

       •   The MW quantity of Large Load assigned to a specific LSE (or assigned directly to
           the Large Load should it be able and willing directly to take on the obligation) in a
           specific zone, and
       •   Identity of the Large Load (not necessarily meter level data at time of
           procurement)

Below is a flow chart conceptualizing how the information would flow to determine the RBP
procurement target via LSE subscription.

At the start of each Delivery Year, the registry would confidentially capture the Large Load
meter level information (or other unique identifier information as appropriate under state
law) to facilitate appropriate billing and collateral tracking to accommodate Large Load
switching LSEs in retail choice states and any Large Load corporate ownership changes.

                                               2
                                                                                    ATTACHMENT




Settlement

The RBP commitment is fixed at the time of the procurement. LSEs who subscribed receive
their MW allocation of committed resources. Although the MW quantity may vary over time
to account for the varying in-service dates of the resources committed, the obligation to
pay for the committed resources is fixed at the time of procurement. This obligation can be
transferred to a different LSE should the Large Load change suppliers, subject to any PJM
credit requirements associated with such transfers.

During the Delivery Year, LSEs could use PJM subaccounts to enable PJM billing to separate
costs for individual Large Loads to best enable the LSE to allocate costs to the right retail
entity via Tariff or contract, limiting the potential for cost shifts to unrelated retail
customers.

Under this subscription model, RBP obligations would be settled separately from RPM but
structured to net appropriately for the correct LSE and avoid double payment for
overlapping capacity obligations with the same MWs of load being represented in both RPM
and RBP.

Below is a flow chart conceptualizing how, after the information flows to establish the
procurement target, PJM would bill for the RBP obligation. Note the credit requirement
proposed below attaches to the LSE at the time of the RBP commitment, and adjusts over
time. This is not depicted in the flow chart.



Credit Requirement

Subscribing LSEs (or Large Loads if they directly subscribed) are required to post collateral
to ensure that, in the event of a subscribing LSE RBP commitment buyer default, other LSE
subscribers and other PJM market participants are largely insulated from the costs of
assuming the obligation. The Coalition proposes that a credit requirement be established
that ensures that any emerging buyer default exposure is recognized early, funded
continuously, and contained entirely within the LSE buyer who subscribed to the RBP MWs
(or received the transferred RBP obligation) over time.



RBP Clearing Constraints

The Coalition proposes two clearing constraints for the RBP: (1) a maximum volume-
weighted average procurement price, and (2) locational commitment requirement.
                                              3
                                                                                 ATTACHMENT




Maximum Volume Weighted Average Procurement Price

The RBP must appropriately compensate resources for taking on RBP commitments,
including the risk associated with taking on those commitments. However, there must be
reasonable boundaries placed on the overall costs arising from this procurement. Since
the auction is not structured to allow load to submit buy-bids indicating their true
willingness to pay, the auction clearing must contain an upper limit on LSE cost exposure
to further derisk the potential for and impact of cost-shifting.

The Coalition proposes a maximum volume-weighted average procurement price cap using
Point A of the VRR curve applicable for the 2028/29 Delivery Year, which is approximately
$555/MW-day. This is based on (maximum of (1.15 * Gross CONE minus 75% of the EAS
offset and 0.2 *Gross CONE)). PJM would commit the resources by ranking the offers by
volume-weighted price (in $/MW-day, averaged across the contract term based on the
resource’s in-service date) and accepting each offer sequentially until the procurement
target is met or price cap is breached.

Example: Target = 1,000 MW.

O1: 250 MW @ $475

O2: 250 MW @ $500

O3: 250 MW @ $525

O4: 250 MW @ $600

All accepted if weighted avg ≤ $555.

If O1 instead was priced at $500, O4 is excluded.

Under this clearing constraint approach, the procurement may fall short of the nominal
target if accepting additional supply would violate the average volume-weighted price
maximum. However, this approach acknowledges that resource offers, factoring in the
uncertainty inherent in the RBP requirements and timing, may result in offers that exceed
$555/MW-day. Higher and lower committed offers are acceptable as long as the total
procurement average cost is ≤$555/MW-day.




                                             4
                                                                                     ATTACHMENT




Locational Commitment Requirement

The amount of RBP capacity procured within rest-of-RTO for delivery into the combined
MAAC and DOM LDAs cannot exceed a maximum threshold. The Coalition suggests a 500
MW value may be appropriate for this constraint, subject to further analysis and
coordination with PJM to determine the appropriate MW value for this constraint. The
purpose of this locational commitment constraint is to mitigate a scenario where supply
resources procured through the RBP are located far from the large load it is intended to
serve, potentially reducing the real-time reliability benefits to that area associated with the
new resource. In other words, the Large Load could be located in the MAAC and DOM LDAs
yet all the RBP committed supply could be in the western part of PJM. This would result in
some MAAC and DOM LDA price separation in RPM auctions, exposing all load in those
LDAs to higher prices. It also could result in increased RTEP costs over time as PJM
planning identifies needs to address transmission reliability constraints.



Current Tariff Provisions for Reliability Backstop Mechanism

The current PJM Tariff provisions for Reliability Backstop Mechanism will be adjusted to not
apply until the 2030/31 Delivery Year such that any triggering of it would occur no earlier
than after PJM has cleared three consecutive BRAs where the threshold for the backstop
has been met. (ie., the 2020/31 DY BRA clearing short would be the first Delivery Year that
would be counted to determine if the threshold were met).




                                               5
                                                                              ATTACHMENT




The example below is intended to illustrate conceptually how the registry could be
used to facilitate the RBP. This example is illustrative, and for simplicity the MW
values are small for computational ease.




                                           6
